analysis.one_liner: Bars credit card companies from raising your interest rate because of problems on unrelated accounts.
analysis.headline: A one-sponsor bill to ban universal default on credit cards drew no cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died in the Senate Banking Committee when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped credit card companies from raising the interest rate on your card because of bad news somewhere else — a late payment on a different card, a dip in your credit score — unless the problem was directly about that account. It would also have protected promotional low rates from being canceled for those same outside reasons, and required card companies to say so clearly on statements. The bill was introduced by Senator Jon Tester, sent to the Senate Banking Committee, and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders, especially people carrying a balance, would gain. The bill would stop issuers from raising the interest rate on a card because of adverse information about the person from anywhere else — a late payment on a different card, a dip in their credit score — rather than anything they did on that specific account. It would also block issuers from ending or raising a promotional introductory rate for those same outside reasons, and would require issuers to state this protection clearly on regular statements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card holders with existing balances

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a creditor from using any adverse information about a consumer — including anything in a credit report or a change in the consumer's credit score — as the basis for raising the interest rate on that consumer's credit card account, unless the reason is the consumer's own actions on that specific account.

Also bars issuers from removing or increasing a promotional introductory rate for those same outside reasons, protecting people who took a card at a low teaser rate and then saw it raised because of events unrelated to the card.
Requires the limitation to be clearly and conspicuously described to the consumer in required disclosures and statements, so cardholders know the protection exists.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers would bear the cost: they could no longer raise rates on an existing card because of late payments, score drops, or other adverse information tied to other accounts or unrelated events. Lenders argued this kind of rule forces them to price risk upfront instead, which could mean somewhat higher starting rates or tighter approval for all new cardholders.

drawbacks.text: Lenders price risk across their book of customers; a rule barring them from repricing based on new information about a borrower could lead them to charge higher starting rates to everyone or approve fewer applicants, spreading the cost to people who never miss a payment.

The bill was narrow — it addressed one repricing practice on open-end credit card accounts — and drew no cosponsors and no committee action, so it was never tested, debated, or improved in either chamber.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For cardholders carrying a balance, the protection was real and concrete: their rate could not be jacked up because of a late payment on a different card or a credit score dip unrelated to the account, and their promotional rate could not be pulled for the same reasons. The main cost, which the bill's sponsors would have had to answer in debate, is that lenders unable to reprice on new information may price more risk into the starting rate for all borrowers. The larger problem is that the bill never got that debate — it had a single sponsor, no cosponsors, and no committee action, so its design was never examined and its protection never arrived.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tester introduced the bill on February 9, 2009; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day.
No cosponsors ever joined the bill over the life of the Congress.
The bill received no further action after referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and died when the 111th Congress ended.

The bill would have amended the Truth in Lending Act to bar creditors from raising a credit card's interest rate based on adverse information from outside the account, such as a credit report or a change in the consumer's credit score.
It would have required credit card issuers to clearly and conspicuously describe this limitation to consumers in required disclosures and statements.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers came out ahead: they kept the ability to raise rates on existing balances based on a customer's credit history elsewhere. Cardholders gained nothing from this bill, which never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers kept the status quo

for.name: Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; the bill was read twice and referred to committee the day it was introduced.

against.name: Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: The committee took no further action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled in the two years before the Congress ended.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banking industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on raising rates based on borrowers' overall credit profiles during the 2009 credit card reform debate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, and it never reached a vote, so no partisan split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill targeted the practice of 'universal default' — raising the rate on one card because of adverse information about the customer elsewhere, such as a late payment on a different account or a lower credit score. Blocking that removes a tool issuers used to reprice existing balances upward; because cardholders typically cannot refinancing away from a rate hike easily, the cost of these hikes falls directly on borrowers.
